set-01-A-001.why: The left ventricle receives most of its coronary flow during diastole because contraction compresses vessels within its wall. Local arterioles dilate when oxygen delivery falls short of myocardial demand.

notes.A: In early systole the contracting left ventricle compresses its intramural vessels, so left coronary inflow is at its lowest; most LV flow occurs in diastole.
notes.B: When myocardial oxygen supply is inadequate, local signals including adenosine relax coronary arterioles and increase blood flow.
notes.C: Hypothermia lowers myocardial metabolism and oxygen demand, so coronary flow falls.
notes.D: Direct α-adrenergic effects mildly constrict coronary vessels, but the rise in heart rate and contractility raises O₂ demand, and metabolic vasodilation wins, so flow increases.
notes.E: Within the autoregulatory range, a pressure rise elicits arteriolar constriction that keeps steady-state flow approximately constant.

notes.A: At rest most ventricular filling is passive; atrial contraction adds only about 20-30% at the end of diastole (more at high heart rates).
notes.B: During isovolumetric relaxation all four valves are closed, and filling begins when ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure.
notes.C: A third heart sound comes from rapid early filling vibrating the ventricular wall and can be normal in children, young adults, athletes and pregnancy.
notes.D: Filling depends on atrial pressure exceeding ventricular pressure, not on atmospheric pressure.
notes.E: The rapid filling phase in early diastole delivers most of the filling volume; later filling (diastasis) is slow.

notes.A: Arteriolar dilation transmits more arterial pressure to the capillaries, raising capillary hydrostatic pressure and filtration.
notes.B: On standing, the column of blood adds gravitational pressure to leg capillaries, increasing filtration (hence ankle swelling).
notes.C: Blocking lymphatic drainage causes oedema by preventing return of filtered fluid and protein, without directly increasing capillary hydrostatic pressure.
notes.D: An obstructed vein raises pressure upstream in the capillary bed, increasing the outward force on fluid.
notes.E: Low plasma albumin lowers plasma oncotic pressure, so less fluid is held in the capillaries and net filtration increases.

set-01-A-005.why: As the cuff deflates, the first Korotkoff sound marks systolic pressure and disappearance usually marks diastolic pressure. The sounds arise locally as the pulse distends the partly compressed artery.

notes.A: Pulsatile movement of the compressed brachial artery produces vibrations that reach the stethoscope through the surrounding tissue.
notes.B: The first tapping sounds (phase I) appear when cuff pressure falls just below systolic pressure and blood starts to spurt through.
notes.C: Diastolic pressure is taken at the disappearance of sounds (phase V), or muffling (phase IV) in some cases, not at the loudest sounds.
notes.D: The palpatory method usually reads lower, because a pulse can be felt only a little after flow restarts; auscultatory systolic readings tend to be higher.
notes.E: A larger arm needs a wider inflatable bladder because a narrow cuff requires excessive pressure to compress the artery.

notes.A: Exercise raises sympathetic outflow to increase heart rate and contractility.
notes.B: During excitement, central autonomic pathways increase sympathetic activity, accelerating the sinoatrial pacemaker and increasing the force of ventricular contraction.
notes.C: Hypotension reduces baroreceptor firing, which disinhibits the vasomotor centre and increases sympathetic outflow.
notes.D: Emotional inputs from the limbic system and hypothalamus excite the pressor area of the medullary vasomotor centre.
notes.E: A sudden rise in blood pressure increases baroreceptor firing, which reduces sympathetic drive and increases vagal tone (the baroreceptor reflex), slowing the heart.

notes.A: Electrical events come before mechanical ones; the QRS complex comes just before ventricular contraction.
notes.B: The T wave records ventricular repolarisation as the muscle cells recover electrically after depolarising and contracting.
notes.C: The P wave is atrial depolarisation; the PR interval spans atrial depolarisation plus conduction through the AV node and His-Purkinje system.
notes.D: The QT interval (QRS onset to T-wave end) is ventricular electrical systole, which roughly matches the ventricular action-potential duration; it shortens as heart rate rises, hence the corrected QTc.
notes.E: R-R intervals shorten in inspiration and lengthen in expiration (sinus arrhythmia), reflecting changes in vagal tone.

notes.A: With velocity held constant, reducing vessel diameter lowers the Reynolds number and makes turbulent flow less likely.
notes.B: At the same velocity, diameter and viscosity, lower density reduces inertial forces relative to viscous forces.
notes.C: Slower blood exerts smaller inertial forces relative to viscosity, reducing the tendency for flow disturbances to grow.
notes.D: Reducing viscosity weakens the forces that damp disturbances in flowing blood and therefore increases the Reynolds number.
notes.E: Anaemia lowers viscosity and raises cardiac output (velocity), so turbulence and flow murmurs become more likely.

notes.A: At a fixed muscle length, an increase in available calcium can strengthen contraction through a change in activation.
notes.B: The relation is not exponential; tension peaks at optimal length and falls with overstretch.
notes.D: Coronary perfusion delivers oxygen to working muscle, whereas ventricular filling stretches the muscle before it contracts.
notes.E: Raising the pressure against which a muscle contracts increases its load and generally reduces shortening at a given initial length.

notes.A: Sinoatrial pacemaker cells generate their own impulses, so removing nerves does not abolish the heartbeat.
notes.C: Rate can still change through circulating adrenaline, temperature and stretch of the SA node.
notes.D: Denervation removes rapid autonomic adjustments of heart rate and force during changes in demand.
notes.E: Heart sounds arise from mechanical events associated with valve closure and persist in a beating denervated heart.

notes.A: Work done per minute measures cardiac power, which depends on both the pressure generated and the volume pumped.
notes.C: Cutting the aorta changes arterial pressure and venous return, so the bleeding rate cannot define normal cardiac output.
notes.D: Stroke volume multiplied by heart rate gives cardiac output at rest as well as during exercise.
notes.E: The volume a single ventricle delivers to its circulation gives cardiac output when expressed per minute.

notes.A: The atrioventricular valve closes before the outflow valve opens, allowing pressure to rise without backward flow.
notes.C: An open mitral valve with a closed aortic valve permits filling during diastole.
notes.D: Pressure differences move the valve leaflets, so valve position can be predicted without knowing sympathetic activity.
notes.E: Closure of both left-sided valves allows ventricular pressure to rise while the blood volume remains constant.

notes.B: Intercalated discs are the larger structures that contain gap junctions plus desmosomes; the specific conducting element is the gap junction.
notes.C: Mitochondria make the energy needed for contraction and ion pumping, while electrical current crosses between cells through membrane channels.
notes.D: The Golgi apparatus modifies and sorts proteins inside each cell and provides no route for current between neighbouring myocytes.
notes.E: Calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum activates contraction within a myocyte after its membrane depolarises.

notes.A: Carbon dioxide accumulates in active tissue and contributes to local arteriolar dilation, increasing perfusion.
notes.B: A fall in tissue pH signals increased local metabolism and promotes relaxation of systemic resistance vessels.
notes.C: Local warming increases cutaneous blood flow through vasodilation, helping the skin transfer heat to its surroundings.
notes.E: Endothelial nitric oxide raises cyclic guanosine monophosphate in vascular smooth muscle, which promotes relaxation.

notes.A: Stretch of atrial myocytes promotes release of atrial natriuretic peptide, which increases renal sodium excretion.
notes.B: Ventricular contraction creates the pressure gradient that drives flow around both circulations.
notes.C: The septa separate the right and left chambers, keeping pulmonary and systemic blood streams largely separate in the normal adult heart.
notes.E: Low-pressure receptors in the atria sense changes in filling, allowing reflex adjustments to circulating volume.

notes.A: Pulmonary arteries bring mixed venous blood to the lungs, whereas pulmonary veins carry blood oxygenated at the alveoli.
notes.B: The myocardium extracts a large fraction of its oxygen supply, leaving coronary sinus blood poorer in oxygen than mixed venous blood.
notes.C: Aortic flow is slightly MORE, because bronchial and Thebesian venous blood drains into the left heart (a small physiological shunt).
notes.E: In most systemic tissues, falling tissue oxygen promotes local arteriolar dilation and therefore increases oxygen delivery.

set-01-B-011.why: Nodal cells, conducting fibres and working myocytes all generate action potentials. The surface electrocardiogram chiefly reflects the summed activity of atrial and ventricular muscle, while electrodes within the heart can record signals from specialised conducting tissue.

notes.A: Spontaneous depolarisation of sinoatrial nodal cells produces the impulse that normally establishes the heart rhythm.
notes.B: The atrioventricular node produces calcium-dependent action potentials as it conducts impulses slowly between atria and ventricles.
notes.C: Electrical activation of working atrial and ventricular myocytes supplies the main signals visible on a surface electrocardiogram.
notes.D: The bundle of His carries electrical impulses towards the bundle branches and has a signal measurable with an intracardiac electrode.

set-01-B-012.why: Working cardiac myocytes contract together as excitation spreads through gap junctions. A ventricle increases force by changing its initial fibre length or the calcium available to its myofilaments.

notes.B: Within the physiological range, increased filling stretches ventricular fibres and increases the volume ejected on the next beat.
notes.C: Calcium released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum binds troponin, so a larger calcium transient can increase active tension.
notes.D: A positive inotropic agent increases the force a ventricle generates at a given filling volume.
notes.E: Adrenaline stimulates beta-1 receptors on cardiac myocytes, increasing calcium availability for contraction.
